opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that it has to be something I'll actually want to look at once it's done. I'm not very interested in making things that just sit in a drawer, so I lean toward pieces that have some function or that I'd be happy to put on a shelf or give to someone: a small dish, a planter, a little figure with some character to it.

The second thing is that it should be achievable within the constraints of the material. Air-dry clay is wonderful because you don't need a kiln and you can just sit down at the kitchen table and start. But it's also a bit fragile, it can crack as it dries, and it doesn't love water. So I look for ideas that work with those properties rather than fighting them. Things that aren't too thin, aren't going to hold liquid, and don't have a lot of delicate parts sticking out.

And then I like there to be a little bit of a stretch. Not so ambitious that I'll get frustrated and abandon it, but with one new thing to figure out, maybe a texture I haven't tried, a different way of joining pieces, or a painting technique. That's honestly a lot like how I think about research problems. You want something where you can see a path to a result, but where there's still something you'll learn along the way.

Finally, I like ideas that leave room for play. Some of my favorite pieces were ones where I started with a rough plan and then let the clay take it somewhere else. For me that's a big part of the appeal. It's a very different mode from my day job, very hands-on, very immediate, and I try to keep it that way rather than over-planning it.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that's a fun question to start with. So I should say, a lot of the time I'm not actually looking for project ideas in the sense of browsing for something to make. The clay is more of a way to shut off the part of my brain that's been doing research all day. So what I'm really looking for is something that lets me get into a flow state quickly, where I'm not overthinking it.

That said, there are a few things I gravitate toward. One is pieces that have some kind of generative or procedural feel to them, where I set up a simple rule for myself and then just follow it and see what comes out. Like, I'll decide every piece has to be built from the same little module, and then the interesting part is how they combine. I think that comes from my interest in generative art and the computational creativity stuff I've worked on. I like when the process has a bit of a system to it, but the output still surprises me.

The other thing I look for is projects that are forgiving. Air-dry clay cracks, it warps, it doesn't always behave, and I don't want to be precious about it. So I like ideas where imperfection is kind of part of the aesthetic. Small sculptural objects, abstract forms, things I can paint afterward. If a project requires precision to look good, I'm probably going to pass, because that's not what I'm there for.

And honestly, I'm drawn to things that are quick. If I can finish something in an evening and have an object on my desk the next day, that's really satisfying in a way that research often isn't, where the feedback loop is months or years. There's something nice about having a hobby where the loop closes fast.
